nodes.label: Dar al-Qand tax repealed
nodes.full: Salah al-Din abolishes the taxes on the raw-sugar store, the sugar market and the refineries in 1171–72.

nodes.label: Amirs’ exemption ends
nodes.full: Al-Nashw cancels the amirs’ exemption from the raw-sugar tax at the Dar al-Qand, 1333.

nodes.label: Fuwayl seizure
nodes.full: Al-Nashw seizes 8,000 qintars of the Fuwayl family’s raw sugar at Mallawi, 1338.

nodes.label: Fustat refineries
nodes.full: Ibn Duqmaq counts 65 refineries at Fustat, 66 in 1325.

nodes.label: al-Fayyum survey
nodes.full: Cane covers 1,468 faddans of al-Fayyum against 29,000 of wheat in 1243.

nodes.label: Mankutamur’s presses
nodes.full: The amir Mankutamur holds 27 sugar presses in Upper Egypt in 1298.

nodes.label: al-Nuwayri’s process
nodes.full: Edge-mill, three straining stages and three-holed ublij cones.

nodes.label: Fatimid Ramadan sugar
nodes.full: Nasir-i Khusraw sees the Fatimid caliph give 50,000 mans of sugar in Ramadan 1047.

nodes.label: Ramadan grant
nodes.full: The sultan’s Ramadan sugar allowance rises from 1,000 to 3,000 qintars in 1344–45.

nodes.label: Black Death
nodes.full: Medicinal sugar sells at 23–27 dinars a qintar to Italians at Alexandria in 1348.

nodes.label: Bedouin raids
nodes.full: The Bedouin attack presses and refineries in Upper Egypt from the later 1300s.

nodes.label: Fall of Acre
nodes.full: The loss of Acre in 1291 ends the Franks’ Syrian sugar lands.

nodes.label: Cyprus’s first works
nodes.full: Cypriot crushing and refining buildings appear after 1291.

nodes.label: Kolossi
nodes.full: The Hospitallers’ Kolossi commandery makes about 800 cantars a year to 1464.

nodes.label: Corner at Piskopi
nodes.full: Federico Corner receives Piskopi in 1366 in return for a 60,000-ducat loan to Peter I.

nodes.label: Cyprus pledges its crop
nodes.full: The king of Cyprus offers Venice his whole sugar harvest as security in 1429.

nodes.label: Kolossi farmed out
nodes.full: The Hospitallers farm the Kolossi harvest to the Venetian Martini from 1445.

nodes.label: Lucera deportations
nodes.full: Frederick II’s wars and the deportation of Muslims to Lucera, 1220–40, empty the Sicilian cane lands.

nodes.label: Frederick II’s letter
nodes.full: In 1239 Frederick asks Jerusalem for two sugar-makers for Palermo.

nodes.label: Norman cane
nodes.full: A confiscated cane estate in 1161 and the Monreale cane mill in 1176.

nodes.label: Falcandus
nodes.full: Hugo Falcandus describes Palermo’s honey canes.

nodes.label: Maredolce
nodes.full: Clay moulds of a small thirteenth-century refinery found near Palermo.

nodes.label: Ruckisio’s company
nodes.full: A master sugar-maker, a merchant and a Jew found a mill in 1356.

nodes.label: Martin’s privileges
nodes.full: King Martin’s tax advantages lift Palermo’s cane gabelle from 100 to 1,000 ounces.

nodes.label: Palermo’s boom
nodes.full: Palermo’s cane lands grow from 16 to 162 hectares between 1393 and 1416.

nodes.label: Water decree
nodes.full: The 1419 decree of Palermo regulates irrigation water for cane.

nodes.label: Granada’s coast
nodes.full: Almuñécar and Motril export sugar through the Genoese in the 1300s.

nodes.label: Real de Gandia
nodes.full: The first trapig at Real is built by Guillem Rana in 1430.

nodes.label: Madeira
nodes.full: Madeira becomes the leading Portuguese sugar supplier after about 1450.

nodes.label: Columbus at Madeira
nodes.full: Columbus buys sugar at Madeira in 1478 for a Genoese firm.

nodes.label: Wang Zhuo’s mill
nodes.full: The Sichuan ox-driven stone mill and sugar-candy method.

nodes.label: Suining candy
nodes.full: In Suining 40% of land is in cane and 30% of households make candy.

nodes.label: Sichuan villagers
nodes.full: Villagers stop making large sugar figures for fear of official demands.

nodes.label: Mongol Sichuan
nodes.full: The Mongol invasion destroys a major source of China’s cane sugar.

nodes.label: Nongsang jiyao
nodes.full: The Yuan farm manual of 1286 includes advice on cane and sugar.

nodes.label: Marco Polo’s Fujian
nodes.full: Egyptian refiners are said to teach Fujian to refine with ashes.

nodes.label: Ibn Butlan
nodes.full: Ibn Butlan’s health tables list sugar.

nodes.label: Byzantine medicine
nodes.full: Symeon Seth and the entry of sugar into Byzantine medicine.

nodes.label: Constantinople’s trade
nodes.full: First recorded sugar trade in Constantinople, early 14th century.

edges: The tax on refineries and the Dar al-Qand repealed in 1171–72 are the Fatimid-Ayyubid forerunners of the 65 refineries that Ibn Duqmaq counts at Fustat in the Mamluk period.
Both are acts of the same treasurer, al-Nashw, to gather the sultan’s share of raw sugar: first the amirs’ exemption in 1333, then the Fuwayl seizure at Mallawi in 1338.
Sato reads al-Nashw’s ride to the Dar al-Qand as showing that the amirs’ raw sugar was taxed there and then refined in their own Fustat refineries, as Ibn Duqmaq lists.
The Fuwayl cane of Mallawi and Mankutamur’s presses are two views of Upper Egypt’s big sugar holdings: private families and iqta-holding amirs alongside the sultan.
The al-Fayyum survey of 1243 and Mankutamur’s presses in Upper Egypt in 1298 both show cane spread beyond Lower Egypt in the thirteenth century.
Sato names plague and Bedouin raids together as causes of the decline of Egyptian sugar after the mid-fourteenth century.
Sato says the Ayyubid and Mamluk sultans followed the Fatimid caliphs in giving sugar in Ramadan, as al-Maqrizi describes for al-Nasir Muhammad.
Al-Nuwayri’s mills, cauldrons and ublij cones are the equipment that Sato says sultans, amirs and merchants installed in the Fustat refineries.
Ouerfelli argues that the loss of Acre in 1291 and of the Syrian sugar lands set the Latins and their Italian partners on building the first Cypriot sugar works.
The Hospitallers of Kolossi, with Syrian workers, are one of Cyprus’s three sugar-makers named by Ouerfelli and start about 1291.
The Corner at Piskopi are the third of Cyprus’s producers, after the Lusignan and the Hospitallers.
The Hospitallers farm the Kolossi crop to the Martini of Venice from 1445 because they cannot sell it themselves.
Ouerfelli: the Venetian hold on Cyprus grew, the Hospitallers lost influence and revenue, and in 1429 the king pledged his sugar crop; the Order farmed its own crop to a Venetian family from 1445.
Frederick II sends for two sugar-makers from Jerusalem in 1239 because the war on Sicily’s Muslims had left the island without skilled hands.
Ouerfelli offers the 1161 estate, the 1176 Monreale mill and Falcandus’s letter together as evidence that cane survived under the Normans.
The Maredolce moulds suggest that sugar was still made at Palermo in the 1240s, after Frederick’s letter.
Ouerfelli sets Palermo’s small thirteenth-century refinery and the master-maker company of 1356 as stages in the town’s sugar revival.
King Martin’s tax privileges brought nobles and officials into cane and Palermo’s plantations grew from 16 to 162 hectares.
The spread of cane across vineyards and gardens led to the quarrel over irrigation water that the 1419 decree tried to settle.
The master-maker companies of the 1350s are the earlier form of enterprise that Palermo’s noble capitalists displaced after 1393.
Ouerfelli’s chapter on the Genoese in the kingdom of Granada ends with the new perspectives of Atlantic trade that opened from there in the fifteenth century.
Ouerfelli’s chapter heading is ‘Valence adopte l’exemple sicilien’: Valencia’s trapigs follow the Sicilian model.
Columbus’s trip to Madeira in 1478 to buy sugar for the Genoese shows the Atlantic island supply that had grown after 1450.
Wang Zhuo’s treatise is the source for both the Sichuan mill and method and the scale of Suining’s candy industry.
The same treatise reports the villagers who gave up making big sugar figures for fear of official demands.
Mazumdar says that the Mongol invasion destroyed a major source of cane sugar in Sichuan, the area of Wang Zhuo’s Suining.
Mazumdar reads the Yuan farm manual of 1286 as part of an effort to rebuild sugar after the devastation of Sichuan.
The Yuan state tried to raise sugar output both with the 1286 manual and, according to Marco Polo, with artisans from Egypt.
Symeon Seth trained under Ibn Butlan at Antioch and his Handbook of Health partly translates Ibn Butlan’s Taqwim.
The abstract contrasts the medical use of sugar at Byzantium from the late eleventh century with its trade in Constantinople, first documented in the early fourteenth.
